title: Vid
theme: English eat splits into two Bosnian verbs, one open along the way and one sealed when the plate is done.

whyHere.heading: Why you are here
whyHere.body: Today you learn why Bosnian often needs two doing-words for one English verb. English says eat for the ongoing plate and for the empty plate, but Bosnian splits that work. Jesti is eat along the way, and pojesti is eat up when the whole thing is done. You already have the present who-map from Chapter 8, and this chapter is only the finish-line. Schools call the split vid, which means aspect, and you can keep saying open versus done and still be right.

englishLies.heading: Why English lies
englishLies.body: English lies because one verb covers both habits. I eat bread can mean a habit, a bite in progress, or a finished meal, and English leans on extra words like up or finished when it cares. Bosnian builds the finish into a second verb, so piti is drink along the way and popiti is drink up. Raditi is work or do along the way, and uraditi is get it done. The pair is not past tense. It is whether the action is open or sealed.

knownLine.heading: A line you already say
knownLine.body: Book 1 already gave you Ana’s line Želim kahvu, which means I want coffee. Wanting sits outside today’s twin pick. When Amira is mid-cup she says Pijem kahvu, which means I am drinking coffee. That is the open twin of piti. The sealed twin is popiti, the drink-it-up verb Emir uses when he says Popij kahvu. Today you only need the shock that piti and popiti are a pair. Past endings wait for Chapter 10.
knownLine.speaker: Amira

pattern.heading: The pattern
pattern.body: Think of an open film versus a sealed photo. The open verb covers habits and action in progress, and the sealed verb covers the whole event with a finish line. Coffee uses piti while the cup is open and popiti when the drink is meant to be finished, and bread uses jesti and pojesti the same way. Work uses raditi along the way and uraditi when the job should be done, and going uses ići on the road and otići when leaving is the whole trip. Prefixes like po-, u-, and o- often mark the sealed twin, but you learn pairs, not a fake math rule. Keep the Chapter 8 who-endings on whichever twin you pick, because the finish-line is a different system from who.

howYouGuess.heading: The pests
howYouGuess.body: Two pests will trip English ears today. The first pest is translating every English present with a sealed verb because it feels more complete. Pijem kahvu is normal for a cup in progress. Popijem kahvu picks the sealed twin and usually looks ahead to a finished cup, not a sip in progress. Popij kahvu is the finish command on that same sealed twin. The second pest is hunting a sealed twin for every word on day one. Some verbs live mostly open, and some pairs you just memorize with coffee and bread. Do not invent fake prefixes. Learn the town pairs first.

trick.heading: The bit that tricks you
trick.body: The trap is to call the sealed verb past tense. Pojesti is still a doing-word about finishing, not a time machine by itself. Past tense hangs sam and gender endings on top, and that is tomorrow. The other trap is to force English up onto every Bosnian line. Sometimes Bosnian picks the open verb for a habit even when English would say finished. Listen for open versus done, not for a magic English particle.

nerd.heading: Why it's like this
nerd.body:
Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. It cared a lot about time on the verb, and later English kept that habit with will, did, and have. English never built a clean open-versus-done twin system the way Bosnian did. Particles like up and out are a different patch. Eat up is a clue, not a full system.

Bosnian kept the twin system. Schools call it vid, which means aspect. Slavic languages treat the finish-line as basic furniture, the way English treats tense. That is why one English eat becomes jesti and pojesti. Today's coffee and burek are the same objects from Book 1. The new work is picking the twin.

next.body: You now know why jesti and pojesti both translate eat, and why the sealed twin is not automatically past. Chapter 10 hangs sam and the gender endings -o, -la, and -lo on those same verbs. Emir was there and Ana was there will finally split on the doing-word.
